walkthroughs.body_html:
Curves tell a story.

The reaction starts fastest: concentrations are highest, so collisions are most frequent. The curve is steepest at time = 0.

As reactants are used up, the curve levels off. A flat line means the reaction has stopped — one reactant has run out.

The initial rate (steep start) is usually bigger than the mean rate (average over all time).

A catalyst gives reactants an alternative route with a lower activation energy.

So more collisions per second have enough energy → faster rate.

The catalyst is not used up — it comes out at the end ready to be used again. It doesn't change the yield, just how fast you get there.

Examples: iron in the Haber process, vanadium(V) oxide in the contact process, enzymes in living things.

Imagine you want acid + marble to react as quickly as possible. Pick the best variable for each lever:

Acid: use the most concentrated acid (most particles per dm³).

Marble: use a fine powder (largest surface area).

Temperature: warm it up — more energetic, more frequent successful collisions.

Catalyst: add one if available — lower activation energy.

mcqs.q: On a reaction graph, why is the curve usually steepest at the beginning?
options: The thermometer is warmest then
Reactant concentrations are highest, so collisions are most frequent
The catalyst is fresh
Products haven't formed yet, so there's no slowing

mcqs.q: Which statement about a catalyst is FALSE?
options: It lowers the activation energy
It is not used up
It increases the yield of product
It speeds up the rate of reaction

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
The reactants get colder because they lose mass as energy.

mcqs.q: In an exothermic reaction, what happens energetically with the bonds?
options: The reactants get colder because they lose mass as energy.
Energy released forming new bonds exceeds energy absorbed breaking existing bonds.
Bond breaking releases energy and bond making absorbs energy.
Higher temperature increases the concentration of the reactants.

mcqs.q: Why does increasing temperature increase the rate of reaction significantly?
options: Particles collide much more frequently at higher temperature, which is the main reason for the rate increase.
Higher temperature increases the concentration of the reactants.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
Mainly because a much larger fraction of collisions have energy at least equal to the activation energy; collision frequency increases only slightly.

mcqs.q: Without catalyst, a reaction has activation energy 90 kJ/mol. The catalyst lowers it by 35 kJ/mol. What is the new activation energy, in kJ/mol?

numericals.q: Without catalyst, a reaction has activation energy 90 kJ/mol. The catalyst lowers it by 35 kJ/mol. What is the new activation energy, in kJ/mol?
numericals.hint: Subtract the reduction from the original Ea.

free_texts.q: A catalyst is not used up and does not appear in the overall equation. What single word describes the catalyst's amount at the end? One word.
free_texts.hint: It looks exactly the same as at the start.
